sweep_summary: Huambisa/Wampis is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Fast 1975 'El acento en la familia lingüística jíbara' (ILV Datos Etno-Lingüísticos 21, Yarinacocha), is on-topic (comparative accent study of Aguaruna, Huambisa and Achuar wordlists) but no open copy exists: Glottolog record 20274 has no link, Fabre's Jivaro bibliography lists it inconsistently (1974 'El acento en la familia jíbaro' vs 1975 DEL-21 'Descripción comparativa de los rasgos distintivos fonémicos'), archive.org has nothing by Fast, and Google Books, OpenAlex, HathiTrust, WorldCat, sil. it is an ILV typescript/microfiche and library-only (priority medium; Peña 2015 does not cite it and says the Wampis system was practically undescribed before him). The best first-hand statement read is Peña 2015 §6.4 (pp. 240-248, held by the project): iambic feet parsed left-to-right, stress and metrical high tone on the second mora in words of more than two moras, high tone on the first mora in bimoraic words, lexical high tones overriding, heavy vowel elision — a mixed stress/tone system. Beasley & Pike 1957 p. 5 ('Stress is phonemic' with minimal pairs) and Jakway 1987 pp. 11-12 (accent unwritten except to disambiguate) are also held by the project.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Moras (vowels; codas weightless, glides non-moraic) are parsed left-to-right into iambic (weak-strong) feet after glide formation and sandhi but before vowel elision; primary stress and a metrical high tone fall on the head of the leftmost foot = the second mora of the (underlying) word in words with three or more moras (e.g. /namaka/ (na.ˈma).ka -> [namák] 'fish', /paantama/ -> [paántam]). Morphologically simple bimoraic words take high tone on the first mora (final mora extrametrical: [ápa] 'father'). Stress correlates: lengthened tonic vowel and lengthened onset of the stressed syllable, plus high pitch; post-tonic weak vowels undergo elision.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Historical/ideal parse given as (CV.ˈCV)(CV.ˌCV)(CV.ˌCV).. with secondary prominence on heads of subsequent iambs, but the synchronic description assigns only one primary stress/metrical high tone per prosodic word; additional surface high tones arise from lexical tone, not rhythmic secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'not completely predictable': roots, affixes and clitics with lexically specified high tone disregard the metrical rule (sec. 6.5, 6.6.4); a few interjections/ideophones; some suffixes and enclitics (e.g. diminutive -t͡ʃi, locative =nVma) induce metrical high-tone shift in non-predicates (sec. 6.6); grammatical high tone marks case (6.6.5); more than one high tone can surface in a word when metrical and lexical tones co-occur.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (minimal word = two moras, one foot, one primary stress, at least one high tone); rule stated over underlying moras prior to vowel elision, so surface forms often show stress on what looks like the final or a closed syllable (namák, kuhánt͡ʃam). Author analyses Wampis as combining a rhythmic stress system with a partly stress-dependent tone system and rejects the 'pitch accent' label; data mainly from Santiago-river Wampis. Earlier Beasley & Pike 1957 (Wachiyacu/Morona dialect) simply call stress phonemic with minimal pairs.
new_statements.identity_note: Peña 2015 describes Wampis (autonym; = Huambisa, ISO hub, huam1247), data mainly from Middle/Upper Santiago river communities (Amazonas, Peru); Beasley & Pike 1957 describe the Wachiyacu (Morona river) dialect. Same language-level glottocode; no separate dialect codes in Glottolog. Note a duplicate copy of the Peña PDF already sits under (Shuar folder).

new_statements.quote: Stress in Wampis is not completely predictable. Nevertheless, I propose that a great proportion of words in Wampis follows a rhythmic pattern that is manifested in an iambic foot structure in words with more than two moras. [...] Rule of metrical high tone assignment in Wampis: A metrical high tone is given to the left-most prominent constituent in the iambic structure. This rule predicts that a metrical high tone occurs in the first foot counting from the left. The foot is right-headed, thus the second mora receives the metrical high tone ((V ˈV́) (V V) . . .).
new_statements.citation: Peña, Jaime G. 2015. A grammar of Wampis. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon. Chapter VI (Prosody), §6.4 'Stress in Wampis'.
new_statements.reading: Word prominence (primary stress plus a metrical high tone) falls on the second mora from the left edge in words of more than two moras — the head of an initial left-to-right iamb, counted in moras with codas weightless (namák, tutúpin, kakáram, kuhánt͡ʃam); bimoraic words take the high tone on the first mora (final mora extrametrical). The system is mixed stress/tone: lexically specified high tones on some roots, affixes and clitics override the metrical placement, certain suffixes shift the high tone, and pervasive elision of unstressed vowels (the old weak positions) obscures the surface count. Stressed vowels and the onsets of stressed syllables are lengthened. This is the first full description of Wampis word prosody; Beasley & Pike 1957 (p. 5) only state that stress is phonemic, with minimal pairs.

sources.note: Full prosody chapter: stress not completely predictable but largely rhythmic; left-to-right iambic (W S) feet over moras; a metrical high tone goes to the head of the leftmost foot, i.e. the second mora, in words of more than two moras; morphologically simple bimoraic words get high tone on the first mora (final-mora extrametricality); acoustic correlates = vowel and onset-consonant lengthening plus high pitch; lexically specified high tone on some roots/affixes/clitics and suffix/clitic-induced high-tone shift (6.5-6.6); argues against a 'pitch accent' label, language mixes stress and tone.
